terms.comment: To lay hold of on all sides: the classical verb for arresting someone (Lewis & Short).
For an arrest Lewis & Short cite only this passage; usually a grasping, or a grasp of the mind.

terms.grammar: phrase: custōdia, custōdiae f. (custody) with in and trādere
evidence: Liv. 22.52: trāditīque in custōdiam omnēs sunt
terms.comment: To be under arrest, in custōdiā esse or habērī (Traupman 194); house arrest, lībera custōdia (Liv. 24.45.8, Lewis & Short).
Classically only to take hold of, seize (Lewis & Short); Traupman’s verb for an arrest.

evidence: Varr. ap. Gell. 13.12.6: in magistrātū habent aliī vocātiōnem, aliī prēnsiōnem (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: Hunc illī ē nāvī ēgressum, cum ad eōs ōrātōris modō Caesaris mandāta dēferret, comprehenderant atque in vincula conjēcerant
phrases.english: As he stepped off the ship to bring them Caesar’s message as an envoy, they had arrested him and thrown him into chains

phrases.latin: Nam comprehēnsiō sontium mea, animadversiō senātūs fuit
phrases.english: For the arrest of the guilty was my doing; their punishment was the senate’s
The police have arrested the thief.

sources: Lewis & Short: comprehendo · Lewis & Short: comprehensio · Lewis & Short: custodia · Lewis & Short: apprehendo
